newsitem.title: JAPAN: Strong "yes" vote, low turnout in Japan bases poll.
newsitem.headline: Strong "yes" vote, low turnout in Japan bases poll.

text.p: Okinawa residents on Sunday convincingly backed a landmark proposal to cut back the huge U.S. military presence on the Japanese island but a low turnout deprived supporters of the clear mandate they sought.

The outcome removes some of the strongest pressure on Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and the U.S. administration to take immediate steps to reduce the size of the forces, but the level of opposition shows that the problem must be addressed at some point, political analysts said.

The Okinawa Prefectural Election Commission said that with 97 percent of the vote counted, 469,770, estimated at 89.5 percent, voted in favour of the initiative, while just 43,672, estimated at 8.3 percent, were against.
Turnout was just 59.5 percent of the 910,000 eligible voters in the plebiscite, Japan's first provincial referendum on any issue.
Supporters of shutting down the U.S. bases had hoped for a turnout of 70 percent to help fortify their campaign.
The non-binding referendum demands the streamlining of U.S. bases on the island and a review of the Status of Forces Agreement, which governs the legal standing of U.S. military personnel in Japan.
Approval was never in doubt since no one, except for a handful of ultra-nationalists, had campaigned for a "no" vote.

But the result failed to settle the one-year-old confrontation between Okinawa and the central government over U.S. bases, sparked last September by the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by U.S. servicemen.
More than 75 percent of all U.S. military bases in Japan are sited on Okinawa, occupying 20 percent of the strategic island in the East China Sea and housing half of the 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan.
Hashimoto has said the Okinawa vote is a major factor in his expected decision to dissolve parliament and call elections, although he need not do so until next July.
Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota, a renowned scholar and survivor of the epic 1945 Battle of Okinawa, led the bitter campaign against the central government to have U.S. bases removed from the island.

"This is an historic moment because it is the first time that Okinawa residents are able to express their will over the military bases, which were more or less forced upon us," he told reporters at a polling station in the provincial capital Naha.
Ota is to meet Hashimoto in Tokyo on Tuesday to discuss the result.
It was not clear whether Ota would continue his campaign to block the forced appropriation of land for U.S. bases here.

Ota lost a Supreme Court decision last month over the land appropriation issue but has so far not declared he would abide by the court's decision. Ota faces two more Supreme Court decisions on the land appropriation issue.

Senior defence and foreign ministry officials from Japan and the United States will meet on September 19 in Washington to discuss details of a plan to reduce some bases on Okinawa, first announced by Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton last April.
Okinawa had opposed the Hashimoto-Clinton plan because of relocation conditions.
Hashimoto is due to meet Clinton at the end of September when he goes to New York to attend the annual opening session of the U.N. General Assembly.
